title: Processes, states and signals
summary: What a process actually is in Linux, how states reveal what it is waiting on, and which signal to send.

sections.heading: A process is more than a running program
sections.html:
A process is an isolated execution context: its own virtual address space, file descriptor table, credentials (UID/GID), signal handlers, cwd, environment and CPU state. The kernel identifies it by PID; the parent by PPID. PIDs are recycled, so a PID alone is not a stable identity — pair it with start time when you write anything down.

Threads share the address space and are scheduled individually, which is why top -H can show several 100% threads inside one process. Containers are not separate kernels: they are processes with namespaces and cgroups, so ps inside a container shows a subset of the host's processes.

sections.heading: States, and what to do about each
sections.html:
State (ps STAT)MeaningPractical response
RRunning or runnableNormal under load; excessive means CPU contention
SInterruptible sleepNormal: waiting on IO, timer or socket
DUninterruptible sleep (usually IO)Cannot be killed, even with -9, until the IO completes — a strong signal of storage problems
ZZombie (defunct)The child has exited; the parent has not reaped it. A bug in the parent, not the child
TStopped (job control or SIGSTOP)kill -CONT resumes
IIdle kernel threadIgnore

Two interview favourites: a D state process ignoring kill -9 (it is waiting in the kernel, so no signal is delivered until the syscall returns), and a zombie (unreapable but harmless in small numbers — it consumes only a PID until the parent exits or calls wait()).

sections.heading: Signals you must know
sections.html:
SignalNumberMeaning
SIGHUP1Hangup; conventionally 'reload configuration'
SIGINT2Ctrl-C
SIGKILL9Uncatchable, immediate termination
SIGTERM15Polite termination request (the default for kill)
SIGSTOP / SIGCONT19 / 18Pause / resume (SIGSTOP is uncatchable)
SIGUSR1/210 / 12Application-defined

Why SIGTERM first: it lets the process flush buffers, release locks, close database connections and remove its PID file. SIGKILL offers no such thing: you get an unclean shutdown, possibly corrupt state, orphaned locks and leaked temp files. The professional sequence is TERM, wait a few seconds, check, then KILL only if it is still there.

# gracefulkill 4242# give it time, then checksleep 5; ps -p 4242 && kill -9 4242

sections.heading: Nice and priority
sections.html:
Nice values run from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest). Ordinary users can only increase niceness (lower priority); raising priority requires root or CAP_SYS_NICE.

nice -n 10 ./batch-job.sh       # start lower priorityrenice -n 15 -p 4242            # adjust a running processionice -c3 -p 4242              # also deprioritise its IO (often the real bottleneck)

Nice affects CPU scheduling only. A process waiting on disk is not helped by renicing — ionice and fixing the storage path are.

checks.prompt: A process is in state D and does not die even with `kill -9`. Why?
options: It is blocked in an uninterruptible kernel sleep (usually IO) and cannot process signals until the syscall returns
checks.explanation: Signals are only delivered when the process returns to user space. A task stuck in D is waiting in the kernel, so nothing is delivered.

why_wrong.2: Root is irrelevant; even root cannot kill an uninterruptible sleep.

options: SIGTERM is the only signal that works on daemons
SIGTERM allows the process to clean up before exiting
checks.explanation: SIGTERM is catchable, so applications can flush data, close connections and remove lock files. SIGKILL skips all of it.

why_wrong.2: Speed is not the point; correctness is.
why_wrong.3: Both need permission to signal the process, not necessarily root.
why_wrong.0: SIGKILL works on daemons too — destructively.

connect.title: Permissions
connect.text: You can only signal processes whose UID matches yours (or as root) — the same ownership model.

interview.q: What is the difference between a zombie process and an orphan process?
interview.a: A zombie has exited but its parent has not reaped it, so its entry remains until the parent calls wait() or exits. An orphan is a running process whose parent died; it is reparented to init/systemd and continues normally.
It adjusts CPU scheduling priority from -20 (highest) to 19 (lowest). It affects CPU contention only, not IO, so it will not fix a process blocked on disk.
